memories.content: Do not exceed two primary HCI contributions.
Name each design or empirical contribution and present it in a single sentence.
In studies recruiting community participants, emphasize the time burden associated with participation.
In studies recruiting community participants, emphasize the travel burden associated with participation.
HCI reviewers find it difficult to identify primary contributions when named design or empirical contributions exceed two.
Emphasize the core design decisions that formative evaluation will change rather than a polished product demonstration.
Emphasize design principles transferable to other similar interactions as the primary contribution, rather than the performance of a specific prototype.
Formative evaluation creates grounds for modification in subsequent iterations rather than definitively determining the superiority of design alternatives.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

analysis.overview: The reference frame governs HCI contribution framing, participant burdens, and formative-evaluation claims, while the compared frame governs prose mechanics, procedural phrasing, evidentiary modality, and authorial voice. These are independently useful policies; no supplied claims address the same operational decision closely enough for a cross-frame relation.

relations.reason: The policy and its reviewer-centered rationale form one reference-only claim about contribution count.
relations.summary: Primary HCI contributions should be limited to two so reviewers can identify them clearly.

relations.reason: This is an independent reference-only formatting requirement for presenting contributions.
relations.summary: Each design or empirical contribution should be named and stated in one sentence.

relations.reason: The memories split one reference-only disclosure policy into two coordinated burden dimensions.
relations.summary: Community-participant study descriptions should emphasize the time and travel burdens of participation.

relations.reason: This is an independent reference-only policy about what formative work should foreground.
relations.summary: Formative-evaluation accounts should emphasize design decisions subject to change rather than polished product demonstrations.

relations.reason: This is an independent reference-only policy about the level at which a contribution should be claimed.
relations.summary: Transferable design principles, rather than a particular prototype’s performance, should be presented as the primary contribution.

relations.reason: This is an independent reference-only constraint on conclusions drawn from formative evaluation.
relations.summary: Formative evaluation should support later modification rather than definitive claims that one design alternative is superior.

relations.reason: The compared-only memories state one punctuation rule together with its interpretive test and rationale.
relations.summary: Em dashes should mark intentional interruption or sharp contrast, reflecting their stronger break, rather than serve as decoration.

relations.reason: The compared-only memories restate one action-first procedural-writing policy and its reuse and comprehension benefits.
relations.summary: Procedural sentences should open with the action, condition, or output so sequences remain reconstructable and steps can be reused or reordered as checklist items.

relations.reason: The compared-only memories provide complementary branches of one evidence-sensitive writing policy.
relations.summary: System behavior should be written as an observed state when field-confirmed and as a conditional plan when not yet confirmed.

relations.reason: The compared-only memories express one preference against uniform mechanical segmentation and explain its readability tradeoff.
relations.summary: Connected clauses should remain in a longer sentence when splitting them would damage an otherwise clear continuous reading rhythm.

relations.reason: This is an independent compared-only policy for consistent authorial voice.
relations.summary: Descriptions of one responsible party should consistently use “I” for an individual author or “we” for a named team.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame alone governs purposeful em dashes, action-first reusable procedures, field-sensitive behavioral claims, sentence rhythm, and consistent individual or team voice.
reports.reference_only: The reference alone limits and formats HCI contributions, highlights community-participant burdens, and frames formative evaluation around transferable principles, revisable design decisions, and appropriately limited conclusions.
